chunks: It walks with the walk of the joyous and proud,
and displays its tail and wings, laughing at the beauty of its dress and the hues of its necklace;
but when it casts its glance at its legs, it crows loudly with a voice that almost reveals its call for help, and testifies to its true grief,
because its legs are thin like the legs of the cross-bred cock.
And from the end of its shin there emerges a hidden spur,
and on the crown of its head there is a green, variegated bunch of feathers,
and the base of its neck is like a goblet,
and its stretch up to where its belly is is like the dye of Yemeni henna,
or like silk cloth put on a polished mirror,
and it seems as if it is wrapped in a black veil;
except that on account of its excessive lustre and extreme brightness, it appears that a lush green colour has been mixed with it,
and along the opening of its ear there is a line like the thin end of a pen in the colour of the daisy, bright white,
so its whiteness shines against the blackness of what is there.
ai.seo_question: What is the metaphorical meaning of the peacock's appearance and behavior in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: Imam Ali employs the peacock as a vivid allegory for the hypocritical elite (Ahl al-Batin) whose external splendor masks internal fragility, a critique deeply rooted in Shia exegetical tradition regarding the disparity between worldly status and spiritual substance. The detailed anatomical description serves not merely as natural observation but as a theological mirror, warning against the 'walking in pride' (kibr) that characterizes those who are oblivious to their own structural weaknesses. This imagery reinforces the Shia emphasis on inner purity (batin) over outward form (zahir), linking physical vanity to spiritual emptiness.

en.sayed-ali-raza: The peacock walks with vanity and pride,
and throws open its tail and wings and laughs admiring the handsomeness of its dress and the hues of its necklace of gems.
But when it casts its glance at its legs it cries loudly with a voice which indicates its call for help and displays its true grief,
because its legs are thin like the legs of Indo-Persian cross-bred cocks.
At the end of its shin there is a thin thorn
and on the crown of its head there is a bunch of green variegated feathers.
Its neck begins in the shape of a goblet
and its stretch upto its belly is like the hair-dye of Yemen in colour
or like silk cloth put on a polished mirror
which looks as if it has been covered with a black veil,
except that on account of its excessive lustre and extreme brightness it appears that a lush green colour has been mixed with it.
Along the openings of its ears there is a line of shining bright daisy colour like the thin end of a pen.
Whiteness shines on the black background.
